- **Nimittāni viparītāni**: Arjuna interprets both physical portents and internal psychological signs as **viparīta** (inauspicious/adverse). When the mind is overcome by delusion (*moha*), even neutral or necessary actions begin to look like portents of impending disaster.

- **Na ca śreyo \'nupaśyāmi**: This introduces the critical concept of **śreyas**---that which leads to true, long-term spiritual well-being or ultimate good (as opposed to *preyas*, immediate pleasure or emotional comfort). Arjuna projects forward (**anupaśyāmi**) and calculates that slaughtering his own bloodlines (**sva-janam**) cannot yield any true spiritual or temporal benefit.

By addressing Kṛṣṇa as **Keśava**, Arjuna appeals to his divine guide while attempting to construct a logical argument for non-action. He conflates his personal emotional grief with moral wisdom, arguing that an act which destroys *sva-jana* (kinsmen) automatically forfeits any possibility of achieving *śreyas* (spiritual benefit, true well-being).

**1.[32](javascript:void(0))   na kāṅkṣe vijayaṁ kṛṣṇa, na ca rājyaṁ sukhāni ca;**

**       kiṁ no rājyena govinda, kiṁ bhogair jīvitena vā.**

+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| I do not desire victory, O Kṛṣṇa, nor kingdom, nor pleasures. Of what use is a kingdom to us, O Govinda (Kṛṣṇa, \"giver of pleasure to the senses\" or \"protector of cows\")? What use are enjoyments, or even life itself? |
+==============================================================================================================================================================================================================================+

**Commentary:** In this verse, Arjuna\'s crisis deepens into a total rejection of the conventional motivations for warfare---power, wealth, and worldly happiness:

- **Na kāṅkṣe vijayam**: Arjuna explicitly renounces the ultimate objective of a warrior---**vijaya** (victory). He strips away the worldly justification for entering battle, asserting that the prize itself holds no value to him if achieved through fratricide.

- **Kiṁ no rājyena\... kiṁ bhogair jīvitena vā**: He questions the fundamental purpose of worldly rewards (**rājyam** and **bhogāḥ**), and ultimately questions the value of survival itself (**jīvitena**). If achieving a kingdom requires the destruction of those with whom one would share its fruits, the reward becomes hollow and meaningless.

- **Govinda**: By addressing Kṛṣṇa as **Govinda** (\"the source of pleasure to the senses/mind\"), Arjuna highlights a deep irony: while Kṛṣṇa is the ultimate source of true joy, Arjuna feels utterly incapable of deriving any pleasure (*sukha*) or purpose from the world under these catastrophic circumstances.

**1.[33](javascript:void(0))   yeṣām arthe kāṅkṣitaṁ no, rājyaṁ bhogāḥ sukhāni ca;**

**        ta ime 'vasthitā yuddhe, prāṇāṁs tyaktvā dhanāni ca.**

+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Those for whose sake we desire a kingdom, enjoyments, and pleasures---they themselves stand here arrayed in battle, relinquishing their lives and wealth.                                                                                                                                                                      |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Commentary:** Having questioned the value of victory in the preceding verse, Arjuna now articulates the psychological paradox at the core of his grief: **the purpose of acquiring wealth and power is to share and enjoy them with loved ones.**                                                                            |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| - **Yeṣām arthe\... ta ime 'vasthitāḥ**: Arjuna points to the tragedy unfolding directly in front of him. The very family members, elders, and mentors for whose well-being one would seek a kingdom (**rājyam**) and material prosperity (**bhogāḥ**) are the exact people standing on the opposing side, ready to be killed. |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| - **Prāṇāṁs tyaktvā dhanāni ca**: Arjuna observes that these relatives have already mentally cast aside (**tyaktvā**) their lives (**prāṇān**) and wealth (**dhanāni**) simply to stand on the battlefield.                                                                                                                    |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| This realization creates a complete logical loop of futility in Arjuna\'s mind: if winning the war requires destroying the beneficiaries of that victory, then the victory itself destroys its own purpose, rendering the entire effort an exercise in tragic absurdity.                                                       |


**1.[34](javascript:void(0))   ācāryāḥ pitaraḥ putrās, tathaiva ca pitāmahāḥ;**

**        mātulāḥ śvaśurāḥ pautrāḥ, śyālāḥ saṁbandhinas tathā.**

+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Teachers, fathers, sons, and likewise grandfathers; maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and other relatives as well.                                                                                                                                      |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **Commentary:** This verse works as a direct grammatical continuation of verse 1.33. In 1.33, Arjuna stated that \"those for whose sake we desire a kingdom\... stand here arrayed in battle.\" Now, in 1.34, he fills out the specific list of who \"those\" people actually are. |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| The passage systematically moves through every layer of the family structure---spanning four generations:                                                                                                                                                                          |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| 1.  **Ancestoral/Elders:** *pitāmahāḥ* (grandfathers), *ācāryāḥ* (teachers), *pitaraḥ* (fathers/uncles).                                                                                                                                                                           |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| 2.  **Peers/In-Laws:** *mātulāḥ* (maternal uncles), *śvaśurāḥ* (fathers-in-law), *śyālāḥ* (brothers-in-law), *saṁbandhinaḥ* (relatives).                                                                                                                                           |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| 3.  **Descendants:** *putrāḥ* (sons), *pautrāḥ* (grandsons).                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| By spelling out every kinship tie, Arjuna emphasizes that this is not an abstract military engagement between opposing states. It is a complete internal collapse of the social fabric, where every generation of his own household is positioned to eliminate the others.         |
+====================================================================================================================================================================================================================================================================================+

**1.[35](javascript:void(0))   etān na hantum icchāmi, ghnato 'pi madhusūdana;**

**        api trailokya-rājyasya, hetoḥ kiṁ nu mahī-kṛte.**

+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| I do not wish to kill these \[relatives\], O Madhusūdana (Kṛṣṇa, \"slayer of the Madhu demon\"), even if I am killed by them---not even for the sake of sovereignty over the three worlds, let alone for the sake of this earth! |
+==================================================================================================================================================================================================================================+

**Commentary:** In this verse, Arjuna takes his stance of non-violence (*ahiṁsā*) to an absolute extreme, attempting to demonstrate total selflessness to Kṛṣṇa:

- **Ghnato 'pi**: Arjuna asserts that even if the Kauravas attack and slay him (**ghnataḥ**), he will refuse to strike back. He presents himself as willing to accept death rather than commit what he perceives as a heinous crime against his family.

- **Api trailokya-rājyasya hetoḥ\... kim nu mahī-kṛte**: He scales the stakes up to the cosmic level. Victory on this battlefield promises rule over the earthly realm (**mahī**). Arjuna rejects this, stating that even if the prize were total dominion over all three cosmic realms (**trailokya-rājya**---heaven, earth, and the netherworlds), it would still not justify the slaughter of his kinsmen.

- **Madhusūdana**: By addressing Kṛṣṇa as Madhusūdana (\"slayer of the demon Madhu\"), Arjuna draws an implicit contrast: Kṛṣṇa slays actual demons to protect the cosmos, but the men standing opposite Arjuna are his own elders and family, not demons.

By rejecting both self-defense and ultimate material reward, Arjuna believes he is adopting a supreme moral high ground, setting up Kṛṣṇa\'s upcoming refutation regarding true *dharma*, the immortal nature of the *ātman*, and the necessity of action.

**The Vedic/Purāṇic *Trailokya* (Spatial Cosmology)**

In the classical Vedic and Purāṇic traditions, the cosmological framework of the *Bhagavad Gītā*, **trailokya** (the \"three worlds\") refers to **three physical-spatial tiers of the Earth sphere**:

1.  **Bhūḥ (Bhū-loka):** The Earthly realm---the physical planet, inhabited by human beings and physical creatures.

2.  **Bhuvaḥ (Bhuvar-loka):** The Atmospheric/Intermediate realm---the region between Earth and the heavens, inhabited by *gandharvas* (celestial musicians), *yakṣas*, and subtle spirits.

3.  **Svaḥ (Svar-loka / Svarga):** The Heavenly realm---the higher cosmic abodes ruled by Indra and the *devas* (celestial beings).

**The Buddhist *Tri-dhātu* (States of Cosmological Existence)**

Buddhist cosmology structures the world (loka, galaxy) of universe (billions of worlds/lokas) into three realms (*tri-dhātu* or *traidhātuka*):

1.  **Kāma-dhātu (Desire or Sex Realm):** Includes hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, *asuras*, and lower *devas*. It is defined by sensory attachment, craving (*taṇhā*) ans sexual divide.

2.  **Rūpa-dhātu (Fine-Material Realm):** The luminous, subtle-form heavens. There is no sex in this realm. By practicing *jhānas* , one train the mind to rise from sex realm being to become Fine-Material being, where final liberation and exit from the universe is achieved. There are four Jhāna states corresponds to four heavenly reamls of fine-material *jhānas*. Jhāna practice is not meant to train the mind to enter **Arūpa-dhātu (Formless Realm).**

3.  **Arūpa-dhātu (Formless Realm):** A non-physical realm of boundless space and emptiness attained through formless absorption training (*arūpa-samāpatti*). Traditionally, this realm was mistakenly believed to lead to liberation. However, with Gautama Buddha's discovery of the Middle Path, neither the *Kāma-dhātu* nor the *Arūpa-dhātu*, but rather the *Rūpa-dhātu* serves as the threshold leading to final and ultimate liberation.

**\**

**1.[36](javascript:void(0))   nihatya dhārtarāṣṭrān naḥ, kā prītiḥ syāj janārdana;**

**        pāpam evāśrayed asmān, hatvaitān ātatāyinaḥ.**

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| What joy could be ours by killing the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O Janārdana (Kṛṣṇa, \"he who protects people\")? Sin alone would take hold of us if we slay these aggressors.\"                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Commentary:** In this verse, Arjuna engages in a subtle legal and moral argument regarding the consequences of violence:                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| - **Nihatya dhārtarāṣṭrān naḥ kā prītiḥ syāt**: Arjuna points out that even if victory is assured, the psychological outcome will not be **prīti** (joy or satisfaction), but everlasting remorse. Destroying his own cousins leaves no emotional room for happiness.                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| - **Hatvaitān ātatāyinaḥ**: The term **ātatāyin** is a precise technical legal term in ancient Indian jurisprudence (*Dharmaśāstra*). Traditionally, six types of criminals were classified as *ātatāyins* (felons/aggressors who could be killed without incurring sin): an arsonist, a poisoner, one who attacks with a deadly weapon, a plunderer of wealth, a land-grabber, and a kidnapper of another\'s wife.                                                                                 |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| The Kauravas committed all six of these crimes against the Pāṇḍavas. Under standard secular or martial law, killing an *ātatāyin* is justified. However, Arjuna argues that a higher moral law (*dhārmic* duty toward elders/family) overrides this legal exemption. He claims that because these *ātatāyins* are his own blood relatives and elders, the general rule does not protect them---slaying them will still result in **pāpam** (sin) taking hold of (**āśrayet**) his mind and destiny. |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| By addressing Kṛṣṇa as **Janārdana** (\"he who protects/sustains people\"), Arjuna appeals to Kṛṣṇa's role as the guardian of humanity, asking how destroying their own lineage could possibly align with divine preservation.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |


**\**

**1.[37](javascript:void(0))   tasmān nārhā vayaṁ hantuṁ, dhārtarāṣṭrān sa-bāndhavān;**

**        sva-janaṁ hi kathaṁ hatvā, sukhinaḥ syāma mādhava.**

+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Therefore, we ought not to kill the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra along with our relatives. For how could we be happy, O Mādhava(Kṛṣṇa, \"Lord of Lakshmi / descendant of Madhu\"), after killing our own kinsmen? |
+==========================================================================================================================================================================================================+

**1.[38](javascript:void(0))   yady apy ete na paśyanti, lobhopahata-cetasaḥ;**

**        kula-kṣaya-kṛtaṁ doṣaṁ, mitra-drohe ca pātakam.**

+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Even if they, their minds overpowered by greed(lobha), do not see the harm(doṣa) in destroying the family or the crime in harming a friend (mitra-droha)---                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Commentary:** This verse forms the first half of a two-part conditional argument completed in verse 1.39:                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| - **Lobhopahata-cetasaḥ**: Arjuna diagnoses the mental state of Duryodhana and his brothers. Their judgment is blinded by **lobha** (intense greed for sovereignty and wealth), rendering them incapable of foreseeing the catastrophic spiritual and social consequences of their actions.                                                              |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| - **Kula-kṣaya-kṛtaṁ doṣam & Mitra-drohe ca pātakam**: Arjuna balances two distinct moral crimes:                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|   1.  *Kula-kṣaya*: The destruction of the family unit, which destroys the transmission of moral traditions (*dharma*).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|   2.  *Mitra-droha*: Treachery against trusted allies and friends, considered one of the gravest transgressions in ancient *dhārmic* law.                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| Because the Kauravas are blinded by greed, Arjuna argues that they cannot be held to the standard of moral foresight. However, this sets up his core dilemma in the next verse: if the enemy is too blinded by ignorance to refrain from evil, shouldn\'t those who *do* possess wisdom (**vayam**) know better than to join them in mutual destruction? |


**1.[39](javascript:void(0))   kathaṁ na jñeyam asmābhiḥ, pāpād asmān nivartitum;**

**        kula-kṣaya-kṛtaṁ doṣaṁ, prapaśyadbhir janārdana.**

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Why should we not know to turn away from this sin/ evil (pāpa), O Janārdana (Kṛṣṇa, \"he who protects people\"), we who clearly see the harm(doṣa) caused by acts that destroy the family?                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Commentary:** This verse completes the logical argument Arjuna began in verse 1.38. It represents the climax of his ethical rationalization for abandoning the battlefield:                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| - **The Burden of Knowledge:** In 1.38, Arjuna noted that the Kauravas are blinded by greed (*lobhopahata-cetasaḥ*), which prevents them from seeing the inherent evil of the war. Here, he draws a sharp contrast with his own side. By using the word **prapaśyadbhiḥ** (\"seeing clearly\"), Arjuna argues that because the Pāṇḍavas possess moral clarity and foresight, they are held to a much higher standard. |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| - **Pāpād asmān nivartitum:** Ignorance might act as a shield for Duryodhana, but Arjuna reasons that if one *knows* an action is sinful/ evil (**doṣam** / **pāpam**), yet proceeds anyway, the spiritual pollution is far worse. Therefore, the only logical and moral choice is to actively turn away (**nivartitum**) from the conflict.                                                                          |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| - **Kula-kṣaya (Destruction of the Lineage):** This is the central moral horror for Arjuna. He frames the war not as a battle for a kingdom, but entirely as a catastrophic act of family annihilation, which he will detail the cascading sociological effects of in the subsequent verses (1.40 onwards).                                                                                                           |


**\**

**1.[40](javascript:void(0))   kula-kṣaye praṇaśyanti, kula-dharmāḥ sanātanāḥ;**

**        dharme naṣṭe kulaṁ kṛtsnam, adharmo 'bhibhavaty uta.**

+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| With the destruction of the family, the eternal family order (*kula-dharma*) perish; when order *(dharma)* is lost, chaos/ unrighteousness (*adharma*) overcomes the entire family as well.\"                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Commentary:** Having established the moral burden of foresight in verse 1.39, Arjuna now begins a systematic breakdown of the social and spiritual catastrophe triggered by war:                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| - **Kula-dharmāḥ sanātanāḥ:** In the Vedic social structure, the family (*kula*) is the basic vessel through which moral values, spiritual rites, and ethical duties (*dharma*) are preserved and passed down across generations. These traditions are called **sanātana** (immemorial/eternal) because they maintain social stability and spiritual continuity.                 |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| - **Dharme naṣṭe\... adharmo 'bhibhavati:** When the adult male heads, elders, and teachers of families are wiped out in a mass slaughter, the living link that transmits *dharma* breaks. With no one left to uphold and teach these duties, **adharma** (lawlessness and moral chaos) naturally moves in to fill the vacuum, engulfing the surviving members of the household. |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| This verse sets off Arjuna\'s detailed argument on the social chain reaction of war, leading directly to his concerns about the breakdown of family purity, social disorder, and the collapse of ancestral rites in verses 1.41--1.44.                                                                                                                                           |


**\**

**1.[41](javascript:void(0))   adharmābhibhavāt kṛṣṇa, praduṣyanti kula-striyaḥ;**

**        strīṣu duṣṭāsu vārṣṇeya, jāyate varṇa-saṅkaraḥ.**

+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| When unrighteousness prevails, O Kṛṣṇa, the women of the family become corrupted; and from the corruption of women, O Vārṣṇeya (Kṛṣṇa, descendant of Vṛṣṇi), arises the confusion of social order (unwanted lineage admixture) (*varṇa-saṅkara*).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Commentary:** Continuing his breakdown of societal collapse from verse 1.40, Arjuna outlines the second stage in the chain reaction of war:                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| - **Adharmābhibhavāt\... praduṣyanti kula-striyaḥ:** In ancient Indian social theory, the stability of the family unit relied heavily on female virtue and household sanctity (*kula-dharma*). Arjuna argues that when male leaders are destroyed in war and *adharma* takes over, social safeguards collapse, leading to moral decay and the degradation of family traditions.                                                                                                                                                        |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| - **Varṇa-saṅkaraḥ:** This term literally means the \"admixture or confusion of *varṇas*\" (social orders). In the classical Vedic framework, maintaining clear occupational and ethical boundaries (*varṇa*) was seen as essential for social harmony and the transmission of spiritual traditions. Arjuna fears that the destruction of war leads to **unwanted intermixing of social classes, unwanted children, and the loss of social/lineage traditions** where duty, heritage, and societal structure fall into total disarray. |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| - **Vārṣṇeya:** Addressing Kṛṣṇa as *Vārṣṇeya* appeals to Kṛṣṇa\'s own noble clan (the Vṛṣṇis), reminding him of the importance of preserving integrity of family nobility and lineage honour.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |


**\**

**1.[42](javascript:void(0))   saṅkaro narakāyaiva, kula-ghnānāṁ kulasya ca;**

**        patanti pitaro hy eṣāṁ, lupta-piṇḍodaka-kriyāḥ.**

+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Such unwanted admixture (*saṅkara*) leads only to hell (*naraka,* realm of torment) ---both for the destroyers of the family and for the family itself; for their ancestors fall, deprived of the ritual offerings of rice balls and water.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Commentary:** In this verse, Arjuna extends his argument from social disruption (1.41) into spiritual and ancestral consequences across generations:                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| - **Saṅkaro narakāyaiva:** Arjuna argues that when social structure and lineage purity collapse (*saṅkara*), the resulting disorder creates spiritual ruin (hell) (**naraka**) for both those who caused the destruction (**kula-ghnānām**) and the surviving family members (**kulasya**).                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| - **Lupta-piṇḍodaka-kriyāḥ:** In the traditional Vedic framework, the spiritual well-being of departed ancestors (*pitaras*) relied on periodic offerings of food (*piṇḍa,* rice balls) and water (*udaka*) performed by qualified male descendants (*śrāddha* rites). Arjuna fears that when lineages are ruined and traditional discipline is lost, these rituals will cease (**lupta**), causing the ancestors to \"fall\" (*patanti*) from higher heavenly realms due to neglect. |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| Through this reasoning, Arjuna builds a complete case against the war---arguing that it brings psychological sorrow (1.37), moral sin (1.39), social collapse (1.40--1.41), and ultimate spiritual damnation extending even to ancestor generations (1.42).                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |


**\**

**1.[43](javascript:void(0))   doṣair etaiḥ kula-ghnānāṁ, varṇa-saṅkara-kārakaiḥ;**

**        utsādyante jāti-dharmāḥ, kula-dharmāś ca śāśvatāḥ.**

+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Through these violence (doṣa) committed by the destroyers of the family---which cause the social disorder---the order of lineages (*jāti-dharma*) and the ancient traditions of family order (*kula-dharma*) are completely ruined.                                                                                                                    |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Commentary:** In this verse, Arjuna summarizes the cumulative impact of family annihilation (*kula-kṣaya*) on the broader legal and cultural structure of society:                                                                                                                                                                                   |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| - **Utsādyante jāti-dharmāḥ kula-dharmāś ca śāśvatāḥ:** In ancient Indian social thought, moral life was anchored in nested rings of obligation:                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
|   1.  *Kula-dharma*: Duties and spiritual rites specific to a household/bloodline.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
|   2.  *Jāti-dharma*: Ethical standards, occupations, and governance specific to a clan or lineage.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| Arjuna calls these obligations **śāśvatāḥ** (ancient/enduring). He argues that when war causes mass slaughter and *varṇa-saṅkara* (social disruption), the foundational institutions responsible for preserving these duties collapse (**utsādyante**), leaving society in moral anarchy.                                                              |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| - **Synthesis of Arjuna\'s Argument:** Verse 1.43 marks the climax of Arjuna\'s socio-religious argument. He has progressed from personal grief over killing relatives (1.31--1.35) to legal liability (1.36--1.39), family breakdown (1.40--1.41), ancestral suffering (1.42), and now the complete eradication of public order and community ethics. |


**\**

**1.[44](javascript:void(0))   utsanna-kula-dharmāṇāṁ, manuṣyāṇāṁ janārdana;**

**        narake niyataṁ vāso, bhavatīty anuśuśruma.**

+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| O Janārdana, we have heard \[from sacred scriptures\] that for those human beings whose family order (*kula-dharma*) are destroyed, dwelling in hell is inevitable and perpetual.                                                                                                                                               |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| **Commentary**: This verse serves as the emotional and theological climax of Arjuna\'s argument in Chapter 1:                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| - **Anuśuśruma (\"We have heard\"):** Arjuna appeals to traditional scriptural authority (*śruti* and *smṛti*). By stating \"we have heard,\" he emphasizes that he is not inventing these fears; rather, he is invoking established *dhārmic* law regarding the consequences of destroying a family\'s heritage.               |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| - **Utsanna-kula-dharmāṇāṁ \... narake niyataṁ vāsaḥ:** Arjuna connects the social disruption outlined in previous verses directly to cosmic retribution. When family duties (*kula-dharma*) are lost, human beings (**manuṣyāṇām**) lose their ethical anchor, making a fall into hell (**naraka**) unavoidable (**niyatam**). |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| - **Conclusion of Arjuna\'s Dilemma:** In verses 1.40--1.44, Arjuna constructs a complete domino theory of destruction:                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|   1.  War kills the male heads of households -\>                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|   2.  Family traditions (*kula-dharma*) perish (1.40) -\>                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|   3.  Social corruption and *varṇa-saṅkara* arise (1.41) -\>                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|   4.  Ancestral rites (*piṇḍodaka-kriyā*) fail and forefathers fall (1.42) -\>                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|   5.  Clan ethics (*jāti-dharma*) are uprooted (1.43) -\>                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|   6.  Perpetual ruin in hell follows for all involved (1.44).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| Having laid out this inescapable chain of sin, Arjuna sets the stage for his final act of surrender in the remaining verses of Chapter 1, where he drops his weapon and sits down in the chariot, refusing to fight.                                                                                                            |


**1.[45](javascript:void(0))   aho bata mahat pāpaṁ, kartuṁ vyavasitā vayam;**

**        yad-rājya-sukha-lobhena, hantuṁ sva-janam udyatāḥ.**

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Alas, what a great sin/ evil (pāpa) we are determined to commit! That we are prepared to kill our own people out of greed for the pleasures of a kingdom!                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| **Commentary**: Having detailed the socio-cosmic collapse that war brings (1.40--1.44), Arjuna turns his lens inward, shifting from abstract legal theory to intense personal remorse:                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| - **Aho bata:** The paired interjections (*aho bata*) mark a moment of profound emotional agony and sudden self-realization. Arjuna is horrified at the realization that he and his brothers are actively participating in what he considers an atrocious crime.                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| - **Yad-rājya-sukha-lobhena:** Arjuna identifies **lobha** (greed) as the root cause driving both sides to battle. In verse 1.38, he diagnosed the Kauravas as being corrupted by greed (*lobhopahata-cetasaḥ*). Now, in 1.45, he admits with deep shame that the Pāṇḍavas are acting out of the exact same motivation---willing to slaughter their own bloodline (**sva-janas**) merely for the sake of political power and physical luxury (**rājya-sukha**). |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| - **Self-Condemnation:** By stating \"we are determined\" (**vyavasitā vayam**), Arjuna refuses to hide behind the righteousness of their cause. He views the war not as a defense of *dharma*, but as a moral failure driven by selfish attachment, bringing him to the edge of complete paralysis.                                                                                                                                                            |


**\**

**1.[46](javascript:void(0))   yadi mām apratīkāram, aśastraṁ śastra-pāṇayaḥ;**

**        dhārtarāṣṭrā raṇe hanyus, tan me kṣemataraṁ bhavet.**

+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Even if the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, weapons in hand, should kill me in battle while I am unarmed and unresisting, that would be far better for me.                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **Commentary**: This verse represents Arjuna's complete, extreme surrender to non-violence (*ahiṁsā*) and martyrdom on the threshold of battle:                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| - **Apratīkāram Aśastram:** Arjuna declares his intention to drop his weapons (**aśastram**) and offer zero resistance (**apratīkāram**). By removing his armor and bow, he voluntarily breaks the code of *Kṣatriya* (warrior) conduct, which forbids striking an unarmed man.                                                                                    |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| - **Tan Me Kṣemataram Bhavet:** He reasons that accepting his own murder at the hands of the armed Kauravas (**śastra-pāṇayaḥ**) is far more auspicious (**kṣemataram**) than participating in fratricide. In his eyes, dying as an innocent victim preserves his moral purity, whereas fighting ensures karmic destruction and family ruin for everyone involved. |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| - **The Absolute Low Point:** Arjuna believes he is choosing the highest moral posture---passive self-sacrifice. However, Kṛṣṇa views this not as true virtue, but as a temporary emotional collapse born of delusion (*moha*) and cowardice (*klaibyam*), which Kṛṣṇa will confront at the start of Chapter 2.                                                    |


**1.[47](javascript:void(0))   evam uktvārjunaḥ saṇkhye, rathopastha upāviśat;**

**        viṣṛjya sa-śaraṁ cāpaṁ, śoka-saṁvigna-mānasaḥ.**

+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Having spoken thus in the midst of the battlefield, Arjuna dropped his bow along with his arrows and sat down on the seat of his chariot, his mind overwhelmed with grief. |
+============================================================================================================================================================================+

**\**

### Chapter 2 Sāṅkhya Yoga: The Yoga of Spiritual Discernment - The Enduring Nature of the Ātma and Path of Knowledge

***Sañjaya uvāca***

**2.[1](javascript:void(0))   taṁ tathā kṛpayāviṣṭam, aśru-pūrṇākulekṣaṇam;**

**        viṣīdantam idaṁ vākyam, uvāca madhusūdanaḥ.**

+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Sanjaya said: To him who was thus overwhelmed by compassion, whose agitated eyes were filled with tears, and who was sinking into despair, Madhusūdana (Kṛṣṇa, Slayer of the demon Madhu) spoke these words: |
+==============================================================================================================================================================================================================+

***Śrī-Bhagavān uvāca***

**2.[2](javascript:void(0))   kutas tvā kaśmalam idaṁ, viṣame samupasthitam;**

**        anārya-juṣṭam asvargyam, akīrti-karam arjuna.**

+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Bhagava (Kṛṣṇa) said: O Arjuna, whence has this delusion and weakness come upon you at such a critical moment? It is unworthy of a noble (ārya) person, it does not lead to heaven (svarga), and it brings dishonor.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Commentary**: **Ārya** is the state of **divine nobility within mankind (*manuṣya/manussa*)**. It describes any individual of the race of Man who upholds, embodies, and fulfills the sacred lineage of **Ṛta** through moral purity, truthfulness, and spiritual awakening---living as a true heir to the solar source. Here **Ṛta** is the sacred seed, source, and divine lineage of mankind transmitted through the solar progenitor **Manu. Ārya** is the **ontological status of moral and spiritual nobility** achieved when a mankind or human being lives in complete fidelity to that divine origin.                                                                                                                                      |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **The Cosmic Ancestry of Man: Ṛta, Manuṣya, and the Ontological Reality of the Ārya**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| The definition of the **Ārya** (*आर्य*) stands as one of the most vital yet frequently misapprehended concepts in the ancient literature of India. Stripped of modern socio-political distortions and localized racial paradigms, the earliest textual stratum---the *Ṛgveda*---reveals a precise cosmological framework: **Ārya** does not designate an earthly tribe or a localized social class, but rather the state of divine nobility within the broader cosmic race of man (**manuṣya**). It defines those individuals who actively maintain, embody, and fulfill their sacred lineage derived directly from **Ṛta** (*ऋत*)---the divine source, essence, and origin of mankind.                                                                |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Ṛta as the Divine Origin and Seed of Mankind, the cosmic race of Man**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| To understand the Ārya in the Rigvedic worldview, one must first recognize that **Ṛta** is not a mere abstract cosmological mechanism for physical law, but the primordial divine essence from which the highest solar deities and the progenitor of mankind were spawned. The *Ṛgveda* explicitly characterizes the solar deities---including the Ādityas, led by Vivasvān (the Sun)---not merely as guardians of truth, but as entities whose very birth is rooted in this divine essence. They are repeatedly hailed as ***ṛtajāta*** (\"born of Ṛta\") and ***ṛtaprajāta*** (\"produced by Ṛta\"): *ṛtāvānaḥ ṛtajātāḥ ṛtāvṛdho devāḥ\...* \"The divine ones who possess Ṛta, **who are born of Ṛta**, and who grow in Ṛta\...\" (*Ṛgveda* 6.50.2) |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| From this solar deity, Vivasvān---the living embodiment of Ṛta---comes the biological father of mankind, **Vaivasvata Manu**. The very term across ancient literature, **manuṣya** (Pāḷi: *manussa*), literally signifies *\"those belonging to Manu\"* or *\"the progeny of Manu.\"* Through Manu, the divine essence of Ṛta was transmitted as a sacred spark into the mind (*manas*) and lineage of the race of man.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| Crucially, **Mankind** (*manuṣya/manussa*) is not restricted to terrestrial *Homo sapiens*. Cosmologically, Mankind constitutes an overarching universal genus---a vast family of mind-endowed sub-races scattered across the world systems (*loka-dhātu*) of the universe, all united by inheriting a sufficient threshold of the pure primordial race (the Brahma seed). Earthly humans represent merely one localized, dense physical sub-race within this broader cosmic tree of Mankind.
